Striped trumpeter (Latris lineata) is a large-bodied, temperate marine teleost that supports important commercial and recreational fisheries in southeastern Australia and New Zealand. Field surveys and growth studies indicate that adults can achieve a maximum total length of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm], placing this species among the larger representatives of the Latridae family. This ultimate body size is associated with a correspondingly high ultimate wet weight, with the heaviest individuals recorded at 25,000 grams [Wwi = 25,000 grams]. Such substantial somatic dimensions are thought to reflect the relatively slow, protracted growth trajectory typical of long-lived, late-maturing perciform fishes inhabiting cool, productive continental shelf waters. The species exhibits a pronounced sexual size dimorphism in some populations, though the maximum length remains comparable between sexes in most studies.

Reproductive biology in Latris lineata is characterized by a relatively late onset of sexual maturation. Histological analyses of gonadal tissue from wild-caught specimens indicate that the standard length at puberty is 51.9 cm [Lp = 51.9 cm], a size threshold corresponding to approximately four to five years of age depending on local thermal regimes and food availability. This value was derived from samples collected across the species' core distribution and represents the length at which 50 percent of individuals exhibit active gametogenesis. The attainment of sexual maturity at a moderate body size is consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy that prioritizes repeated spawning events over several decades. Juveniles inhabit shallow, reef-associated habitats before migrating to deeper offshore waters as they approach maturity, a movement pattern that may be linked to the onset of reproductive activity.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled aquaculture conditions. At a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], gravid females were observed to release an average of 6,438 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 6,438 eggs per spawning event], producing approximately one such event per day [F_R_i = approximately one such event per day] over the peak of the spawning season. This combination of high fecundity per event and near-daily spawning frequency is among the highest recorded for any temperate marine teleost and likely compensates for high rates of early-life mortality in the planktonic environment. The eggs are pelagic and transparent, measuring approximately 1.3 mm in diameter, and contain a modest yolk reserve that supports the developing embryo through the early cleavage and gastrulation stages before hatching occurs.

The early life stages of Latris lineata are strongly influenced by thermal conditions during incubation. Fertilised eggs maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] complete embryonic development and hatch after a period of 8 days [ab = 8 days], representing the age at birth for this species. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or prolarva, weighs approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams] at the moment of chorion rupture, a value derived from the calculated volume of the spherical egg using the standard relationship for teleost egg density. This minuscule initial mass is typical of pelagic spawners that produce large numbers of small, poorly provisioned offspring. The yolk is absorbed progressively over the first several days post-hatch, with the larvae transitioning to exogenous feeding once the mouth is fully open and the digestive tract is functional.

Longevity records for Latris lineata, derived from tag-recapture programs and otolith increment analysis, reveal a remarkably long lifespan among temperate reef fishes. The oldest documented individuals, primarily males, have been recorded at a maximum age of approximately 15,695 days [am = approximately 15,695 days] under natural conditions at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This exceptional longevity was assessed at a mean water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] across key monitoring sites, reflecting the relatively cool, stable thermal environment of the species' deep reef habitat. The combination of a long lifespan with a high daily reproductive output suggests that total lifetime fecundity in this species is extraordinarily high, a demographic strategy that buffers populations against sporadic recruitment failures driven by oceanographic variability. Such life-history traits underscore the need for cautious fisheries management.
